utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you were saying that the time you're testifying about, that at that time there was no Albanian nationalism. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps there was, but not in the extent to which certain information media depicted it, and public information system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many tens of thousands of Serbs and Montenegrins, under pressure, had to leave Kosovo in precisely that period of time, from, say, 1980 to 1990, following the demonstrations after Tito's death in 1980 and onwards up to 1990?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do know that people were leaving. Now, whether all that was due to pressure, I would say that a very small portion was due to that compared to what the information media would have us believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about the killings, the torchings, the destruction of churches and cemeteries, things of that kind, all forms of looting, pressure, violence, due to which tens of thousands of Serbs left Kosovo at that time?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to specific cases, I really don't know except for the ones that were highlighted by the media. I was only in Kosovo officially once. Otherwise, I didn't travel there. So I can't really testify and say how far that is true. But based on the talks and conversations I had with a certain number of people from Kosovo, both Serbs and Montenegrins who were members of the JNA units there, and on the basis of the conversations I had with many Albanians too, I arrived at the conclusion that, as my own assessment, that this problem was far exaggerated to the advantage of the Serbs; that is to say it was shown that pressure was brought to bear on them and that that was the reason for which they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you're talking about -- actually, you say that you don't know much about it, but nonetheless, you say on page 4, paragraph 3 of your statement, that there was an expansion of Serb nationalism and as an example you quote the relics of St. Sava that were shown publicly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who St. Sava was, in fact?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know who Sveti Sava, St. Sava was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Rastko Nemanjic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was the founder of the Serb church and Serb schools.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the highest Serb saint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, please, do you think he might have been a Serb nationalist, for example?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether nationalism existed in its present format in his time but I knew that his bones and relics were used, were made use of during those years in order to significantly revive Serb nationalism on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. More in the eastern reaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, was that nationalism, this particular activity on the part of the church, would you say, or was it the nurturing and fostering of national cultural traditions?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it was nationalism taking the form of nurturing traditions and reviving memories and recollections of those first days of the first Serbian state during the days of St. Sava himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, fine, General. Very well. Now, as you quote this particular example with Sveti Sava, do you have any other nationalist ideas or ideals that were used which you as an intelligence officer of the JNA became aware of?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I wasn't an intelligence officer; I was a security officer, or as it was called at the time, officer for security. Those are two essentially different functions within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, please, very briefly: How did you as a Yugoslav officer see the victory of the HDZ at the elections in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it as the victory of a party that put forward its programme and platform and for which most of the citizens of the Republic of Croatia opted for in democratic fashion at the democratic elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know which ideals the HDZ put forward at the time, what were the ideas it advocated?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. First of all, it strove for a greater degree or, rather, the reconstitution of the SFRY. That means for different relations within the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did Croatia in any way, in your opinion, at that time, was it degraded within the SFRY in any way?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were different times compared to when the SFRY under a different name in -- in 1945 was constituted. And the international circumstances and situation was different too. Everything was different. The entire socio-political development at the time was different, and some constituent elements of that SFRY left the political arena, and it was normal for the country to be reconstructed and reconstituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And are you aware of the positions taken in 1989 by the HDZ even before the elections with respect to the Independent State of Croatia and so on, things along that line?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps there were things of that kind just as they were in every movement. There must -- there were probably individuals who had unacceptable positions for a bourgeois supervision and constitution of a sovereign and democratic state, but these are my phenomena with respect to the overall desire on the part of the Croatian people and the people who opted for the HDZ party at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As head of security of the 5th Air Force Corps yourself, did you know that in September 1990, in Petrijevci, in the old house of artist Mestrovic, that during the night weapons were being handed out to HDZ members secretly, clandestinely, and part of them were handed over to Mercep for Vukovar, another part went to Orahovac and Baranja?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. It wasn't the area of responsibility of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't communicate amongst themselves, and you didn't receive feedback information as to what was happening on the territory of Yugoslavia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did exchange a certain amount of information, but again others not. In this particular case and cases of this kind, the security service of the JNA was not in charge of supervising the civil institutions but only dealt with state security organs and institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you talk about the military as an officer for security yourself, do you know that in Slovenia at that time, in order to secede, for the purposes of secession, a large quantity of weapons were imported illegally and that formations were set up and that when the attack on the JNA was launched, 40 innocent young men were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's -- rather than have this recital, let's see whether the witness knows anything about this. You've asked other witnesses about it, it's constant repetition. General, can you help? Do you know anything about Slovenia? Was that part of your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, Mr. May, this does come under the responsibility and competence of Mr. Agotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know about the death of these completely innocent young men who had come to do their military service in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read about that in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing more than that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing more than that. And at that time, I was suspended from duty before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did the JNA wish to preserve Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was the preservation of Yugoslavia a responsibility and obligation pursuant to the constitution of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution that was in force at the time, that was the JNA's duties and that was one of its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, you go on to say that the JNA considered the election of new nationalist authorities in Slovenia and Croatia, that this led to the -- would lead to the break-up of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I say nationalist authorities, but I say the new power and authority that be in the republics of Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Do we not doubt that the JNA made a correct assessment of what would happen when these parties came into power, looking at Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically when you look at it from this point in time, then the introduction of a multi-party system into the SFRY without adaptation on the part of the socio-political system of the day, without its adapting to the new system, that is true. But who failed to allow this adaptation to take place in line with the new conditions that were created?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's leave that question for another opportunity, but you go on to say that in that sense the SSNO issued orders that instructed that Yugoslavia must survive at all costs, must be preserved.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that the Slovenian and Croatian leadership --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got a copy of your statement, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't refer to it unless you want to, but if you do, it may assist in following the questions and deal with any discrepancies there may be. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the Slovenian and Croatian leadership, knowing about the Secretariat of Defence order, began to prepare for what they felt would be an attempt, et cetera. That's what you say in that paragraph; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were they preparing for, in fact?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as they -- as soon as the JNA quite obviously had turned towards one side, favoured one side in the conflict on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that is to say the Serb side and the Montenegrin side, at that point in time the logics of the whole situation was that the other ethnic groups that were jeopardised and did not have the JNA behind them to support them had to prepare for their self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it quite the reverse? Wasn't it acts of violence that were started and launched precisely against the JNA and against the Serb population in Croatia? If we take it in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we take it in chronological order, then the first rallies and the first demonstrations and intimidation started out from Serbia and Montenegro, and then the logics of the situation was that the other republics - Croatia, et cetera - were in a situation to begin to prepare themselves, to prepare their own interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't the -- weren't the rallies in Serbia and Montenegro held for Serbian and Montenegrin issues, without mentioning any other republics or problems outside Serbia and Montenegro? Isn't that how it was?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partially correct, because the rallies flew over -- flowed over into other areas of the former Yugoslavia. They spilled over into Croatia, as you well know, and the desire for rallies, which were known as rallies of truth, were to have been organised on the territory of Croatia and Slovenia. So what is this other than an export of one nationalism to other areas, territories?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say the rally of truth, that was the intention of the Serbs from Kosovo, to go to Ljubljana and familiarise the Slovenes with their sufferings and the pressures they were exposed to. Why do you consider that to be nationalism?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were just the vehicles. Only some were individuals from Kosovo. However, in addition to them, there were tens of thousands of other nationalist-minded people who came with them, so that these were not people from Kosovo only. Kosovo was just used -- utilised for that purpose. That is how this was seen in the territories of Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, are you aware as to what happened with the adoption of the constitution of Croatia when the Serbs were thrown out of the constitution as a constituent people and that many were fired from the public service, from the police, even the health service, and there were protests against this in the first place?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partially so. There were individual cases along those lines, but this was not a generalised phenomenon. I can guarantee that with me in the Croatian army there were a large numbers of Serbs and Montenegrins who, from the very outset until the very end fought within the ranks of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what was happening not only on the political arena but also when we're talking about violence, do you know anything about the activities of Branimir Glavas, Mercep, and the others who created a climate and an atmosphere that was based on brutal violence towards individuals and groups of other ethnicities? Isn't that so, General?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. That is partially true. But the violence started out already in the physical sense in the areas in Croatia which were predominantly populated by Serbs. To be specific, in August 1990, the first barricades were set up in those areas and not in areas which were predominantly populated by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is a barricade an offensive means of combat?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A barricade is just the beginning leading up to offensive activities. And this proved to be true because they were followed by offensive activities. Now, if I set up a barricade and do not allow the legally elected authorities to exercise their functions in that area, so surely that is offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But, General, tell me, do you consider Branimir Glavas to be an extremist or not?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather not comment on Mr. Glavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in Croatia, towards the end of 1990 and the beginning of 1991, paramilitary formations were set up by parties and that there was large-scale illegal arming? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partially true. That is, Croatia was preparing itself for defence but not for attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone threatening to attack Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The threats came from the rallies that were spilling over into Croatia, and the demands coming from Serbia in relation to Croatia, that is, for a part of its territory to be seceded from it whereby the territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia was in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a single such demand from Serbia? Are you aware of a single such demand from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of 101, only at this moment I'm just mentioning the demand of General Dusan Pekic and the people holding rallies in Petrova Gora and all over Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to General Dusan Pekic who comes from that area and who was a retired general at the time.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and who has been living in Belgrade for the last 50 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Many generals have been living in Belgrade. But he was a retiree, and he came from that area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know also of the case of Seselj who held rallies in Eastern Slavonia and Baranja - probably elsewhere too, just now I can't remember - and he was not born in the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, he was born in the territory of Bosnia, that is true. And do you know everything about these illegal channels of arming organised by Spegelj, and do you know anything about the Kikas affair?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the so-called illegal channels used by Spegelj, I don't know everything about them. As for Kikas, I know as much as appeared in the mass media regarding his plane, what he brought with it, and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in September 1991. To be more specific, in mid-September. But this was the period when war was already raging in the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that these weapons that were illegally imported in those days were used only in 1991 to kill or to cause the disappearance of 600 Serbs from Sisak, hundreds from Split, Sibenik, Zadar, Gospic, Karlovac and even Zagreb itself? I'm just listing the towns in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll just go through this with a bit of care. You put these allegations, very serious ones indeed, to question whether there is any truth in them, and the witness should have a chance to answer. It's alleged that 600 Serbs -- just a moment. 600 Serbs, it's said, disappeared from Sisak. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about that, Your Honour, Mr. President. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be untrue and propaganda. Hundreds are described as disappearing from Split. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That area was not within my area of work, so I cannot testify about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to make sure that these matters are properly dealt with instead of general allegations being put out without the witness having a chance to answer. The other areas are Gospic and Karlovac. Can you help as to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same applies, Mr. President; I don't know about that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a military commander, and I am not aware of any possible activities that may have been engaged in by someone else, but I do know that after the war, data were presented which were significantly exaggerated. There were individual cases of persecution, there is no doubt about that. There's the well-known case of the Zec family in Zagreb, which is being tried before Croatian courts to this day, but the number that is referred to here I'm convinced is over -- is exaggerated, though I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have the information but you're sure that it is not true. But can we agree, General, these places like Sisak, Split, Sibenik, Zadar, Karlovac, Zagreb are not places in which Serbs held any rallies or set up any roadblocks or barricades, but all these towns were under the control of the Croatian authorities, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those towns were under the control of the Croatian authorities, and in those towns there were no rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, then, do you explain these rather large-scale killings in those towns from that period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If true. He doesn't accept it, so you can't put it as though it's true. There's no need to answer that question. It's not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Are you claiming that all that I have said is not true?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm claiming that I'm not familiar with those data and that I learnt about them from subsequent reports in the mass media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you're talking about the mass media, do you know that the Zagreb Novosti, a newspaper, on the 15th of March, 2002, which means last year - it's a Zagreb newspaper - published data about a collection centre at the Zagreb Velesajam, or fairgrounds, and facts related to this? Do you know about that? Do you know about it contemporaneously or did you learn about it from the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read about it in the papers. I didn't know about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So at the time, you knew nothing about a camp at the Zagreb fairgrounds.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know now that such a camp existed and that many people disappeared in it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said he read it in the paper. There's no point asking him about it. You might as well call anybody to say they read it in the paper. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have to respond to your observation that I could ask anyone about the papers. Mr. Agotic held a very senior position, and he must have known these facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He told you he didn't. He read about it in the paper is the answer. When he says that, there's no point arguing with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that a newspaper called Hrvatska Ljevica published the list of 107 killed Serbs in Sisak? The names. Not just the number but the names of 107 killed Serbs in Sisak.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never read that newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, paragraph 2 of your statement, you say that I kept saying that Yugoslavia should be preserved. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes. I can't find the exact quotation that you have read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm quoting the second paragraph on page 5 of your own statement.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That is what I stated as is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Your president, Stjepan Mesic, when he was sitting where you are sitting now, said that I wanted to destroy Yugoslavia. Now, tell me, please, what is your opinion, what you said in your statement or what your current boss now says, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He cannot comment, even if that's right, and I don't recollect that part of the evidence, but even if it's right, the witness can't comment on what some other witness said. Now, you've seen what you've written in your statement, General. Is that right or not, as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is right, but if we take into consideration the whole sentence, that is from the comma to the full stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just finish. You were going to add something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant was the rest of the sentence reads, "... and also that all Serbs must live in one state." That gives a completely different aspect to the previous part of this same sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, please read out the whole sentence so we understand exactly what it says here.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Vasiljevic was operating in accordance with Milosevic's options because Milosevic kept saying that Yugoslavia must be preserved, and also that all Serbs must live in one unified state."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Weren't all Serbs living in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. All were living in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all the Muslims and all the Croats and all the other South Slavs were living in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct myself. The vast majority of Serbs, Muslims, and all others lived in SFRY. We all have our own national minorities coming from other parts of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct. That applies to Serbs, Croats, and everyone else. And quite a number abroad as part of the diaspora. That is not at issue. But the assessment of the JNA that the Croatian and Slovenian leadership - this is on page 5, paragraph 3 - would use force, was that assessment by the JNA correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessment that they would use force, which was an erroneous assessment, in the period from 1990 until the first half of 1991 in order to secede, this led to the position that the republic leadership in the SFRY, in this case the Serbian leadership, should be supported because it was in favour of preserving Yugoslavia, even in a smaller -- of a smaller size.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you something else. Let me reword that question, because you say here that their assessment was that they would use force. In view of this assessment, was the order to transfer weapons of the TO to JNA warehouses a logical one? Was this done in all the republics?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was logical from the standpoint of the leadership that had sided with one party in the conflict, but it was illogical and unconstitutional to disarm one or two of the constituent nations of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you know very well that the weapons of the TO in all the republics were placed in JNA warehouses in Serbia as well and in Macedonia and in Montenegro. There were even deputy questions addressed in the parliament of Serbia as to why this was being done. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that the weapons of the Territorial Defence in all the republics were fully at the disposal of the leadership of the Territorial Defence. In Croatia and Slovenia, from May 1992, this was not the case. As for the other republics, I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you do not know that this was carried out in all the republics without any discrimination whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time when this order was issued, I didn't know that. That is how this was done in the former SFRY outside Croatia and Slovenia. However, from what I learnt later on, I see that that was not so. In Bosnia, the weapons were not seized from the Territorial Defence. Now, whether they were in Serbia and Montenegro, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the representatives of the Serbs anywhere in the former Yugoslavia threaten that the JNA would be the target of Serb attacks?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say on page 5, paragraph 5 of your statement, that the main task of the second department of the counter-intelligence service of the air force in Zagreb was to arm the Serbs in Croatia. Is that what you claim?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you received information from a JNA member who was leaving, or some members who were leaving the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got this information from them, and I also got the information from the person who was at the head of that particular detachment, the KOG detachment that I mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, did you see these instructions to the effect that these Serbs should be armed and you say that they -- reports of that kind came into the security department?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say they came into the department, but they came from the security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. I put my -- I misspoke then. From the department.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But those instructions or, rather, oral orders were conveyed orally, verbally, as far as I was informed, from people -- the people that I mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, take a look at page 8 of your statement, paragraph 1, because it follows on from what we were discussing and the order of the SSNO and the Chief of the General Staff that all weapons of the Territorial Defence be transferred to JNA depots. Were both Serbs and Croats disarmed on a footing of equality on that basis? And take a look at page 8, paragraph 1, of what you say there. Were they equally disarmed?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear on what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would the legal officer just approach the bench, please. Yes. We've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the units, you say there were mostly young officers from the 5th Corps, and more than 70 per cent of them were Serbs. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of these decisions to disarm, were the Serbs and Croats equally disarmed, to equal measure? What was the object of the order to take the weapons out of the hands of civilians which could have come into conflict amongst themselves? What was the intention? Was it a good intention on the part of the army to prevent a conflict or not?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is just one-sided. Who was disarmed were the legal organs of Croatia. That's who was disarmed. But other weapons from JNA depots were distributed, on the other hand, among Serb villages. So that is the sense of what was going on at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you see anybody's order to the effect that this weaponry should be distributed among the villages?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the man who received that order, that's who I heard it from, and he was very worried and so was I at that time. So that is where I got the information from, and those orders were conveyed orally, by word of mouth. And a second thing that was common knowledge is that at that time in the Croatian press, the Croatian papers wrote about this and it was never denied by the JNA, that two members of the JNA had been arrested carrying full truckloads of weapons in Eastern Slavonia, and they were distributing the weapons among the Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me who arrested them.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were arrested by members of the MUP of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that when Candic testified here he said that they were individual actions on the part of police or military commanders taking things into their own hands? You never saw an order coming from the SSNO or the General Staff or anybody else; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see an order. I've already explained why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: In the other department, were there officers who were ethnic Croats?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two of which one left the JNA and moved to Belgrade. Later on, he was put on trial in Belgrade, and he was given a prison sentence of three and a half years. The second one stepped down from the JNA in the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, please: Did the authorities in Croatia, were they at the time -- did they have a friendly relationship and attitude towards your units?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA units, because you were a JNA colonel at that time.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were well disposed towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any tasks, assignments of any kind as a security officer with respect to protecting your units and everything that went on, everything that came under your duties and tasks?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had the classical type of duty to protect units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Officers who left the JNA, because as you said, the structure underwent change, did anybody throw them out of the JNA or did they leave of their own free will and thereby change the structure of the JNA itself?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two processes. Up until the time I left on the 2nd of July, 1991, a part of the so-called unreliables, unreliable officers were replaced from their posts, and after that, people followed suit and tabled their own requests to leave the JNA and they were granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So independently, they would ask to leave the JNA and did so; is that it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the Slovenian war and in the course of it, people would make these requests themselves and they would receive positive answers quickly. They would be allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they tabled their resignation of their own free will; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that it was just thanks to General Tus who was at that time the chief of the air force that you were able to retain your post in the 5th Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that your superior, Colonel Rakocevic, did his best to have you replaced from that post because, as you say, he wanted in key positions to have people who were, in his opinion, reliable; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he didn't trust you?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that that is so, yes. He never told me as much, but judging by his actions, I came to the conclusion that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was that because -- actually, in view of the fact that as you say he was bent on the idea of preserving Yugoslavia, that he knew full well that you yourself weren't? Was that the reason? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. It's not true that he was in favour of Yugoslavia and I wasn't. Both of us were in favour of Yugoslavia, however, a different variant of Yugoslavia and with different options for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, General - we have to try and save time - did you directly or indirectly participate in the blockade of your barracks and your soldiers? What were your barracks and soldiers until a little while ago? Or, rather, did you know that all the barracks had been blocked in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you take part in it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part directly, but indirectly as a commander of the National Guards Corps at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was it under your immediate command that the JNA barracks in Bjelovar were blocked, and the ammunitions depot in Bjelovar as well as the barracks in Gospic, the barracks in other places as well?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both these blockades were effected while I was the commander of the National Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that that was under your command, General, that this was conducted.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during these blockades and attacks on the barracks 36 soldiers and officers of the JNA were killed? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure of persons killed but I do know that there were casualties on both sides, killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you recall that it was precisely those men under your command, up in front a line of officers detained -- soldiers detained; in addition to the four officers, the brigade commander was also killed?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the brigade commander lost his life, but in what way, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know an event that took place on the Koranski bridge when 13 TO members were slaughtered and massacred, Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know of that particular case. I got to know about it later on from the information media and the trial that was held of the suspects considered to have been the perpetrators and involved in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you yourself have anything to do with that case at all?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, what duties did you perform as an officer of the National Guards Corps? You were at the head of the National Guards Corps, were you not, General?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that within the composition of the National Guards Corps already in the first half of 1991, there were about 500 different foreign members, foreigners from different countries making up the composition?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took over my duties on the 10th of August, 1991, and I do not know which men were taken into membership by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you know that they were there?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that there were some people from the diaspora, Croats. I also know that there were a large number of foreign nationals in the National Guards Corps units later on during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, and how come you as a -- how did you react as a former JNA officer when you got to learn of the fact that foreigners took part in the barracks, JNA barracks and the killings that went on of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't feel this to be at all illogical because they were under the command of Croatian officers, junior and senior, and they had placed themselves in the formations which were in charge of defending the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that within Paraga's HOS units, a certain Scott [phoen] and Major Raj, Captain John Thomson, Lieutenant Dave Hoskins, they were -- gave interviews to Anthony Rogers, a journalist, about the atrocities carried out by HOS. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not read those articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a National Guards Corps officer or, rather, the head of the National Guards Corps, the chief, were you acquainted with the activities of the paramilitary formations in the area of Vukovar, for example, in 1991? Let's take that area.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was partially informed that there were certain attempts at organisation, and some were successful outside the National Guards Corps but that was the beginning of the war and that was the logics of the formation of an army. Relatively very quickly all these units were placed under a united, unified command of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, in connection with the activities of these paramilitary formations, happened in Vukovar in July 1991 before the conflict escalated?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at all any of Paraga's activities in Vukovar? Are you aware of them?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Paraga was in Vukovar at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about his members, the members of his units.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You don't know about that. Fine. And did you have any contacts with the representatives of paramilitary formations from the area?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some parents contacted me whose sons had been killed in the area, and they asked me to help in finding the dead bodies. As to other contacts with these units in the Vukovar area, I did not have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know who Marin Vidic is, nicknamed Billy?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Ferdinand Jukic, nicknamed Yea, was?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet these two men?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met both of them. With Jukic, before the fall of Vukovar, and I met Billy, or Vidic Billy, after returning from captivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know Vidic's statement about the atrocities that were carried out precisely in Vukovar by those who had been appointed by the Defence Ministry of Croatia to take care of the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read about that in his interviews later on. Actually, it was quite recently that I read about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that when you had your meetings with Vidic and Jukic in Zagreb with respect to their requests made to the Defence Ministry that officers be placed at their disposal to command the operations against the JNA -- that's right, isn't it? That's what happened?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to Vidic Billy, I did not meet him in Zagreb on that occasion, but a large number of representatives from Vukovar came, and they asked aid and assistance both in manpower and materiel and equipment. They came to the headquarters of the National Guards Corps to ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that you gave an assignment to Mile Dedakovic, nicknamed Jastreb, and Branko Borkovic too, that you gave them assignments?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, on the 28th or 29th of August, 1991, I issued an order dispatching Mile Dedakovic, Branko Borkovic, and another man, another young lieutenant who was in the engineers corps, to assist in Vukovar defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, and do you know that this particular Mile Dedakovic, nicknamed Jastreb, whom you sent yourself to lead the operations in Vukovar, is directly responsible for the killing of several hundred Serb civilians but also soldiers too?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, is there any truth in that sort allegation, as far as you know, Mr. Agotic? It's put by this accused in his usual way. No evidence of it, as far as I know. Do you know anything? Do you know of any evidence of this? If you had heard of it, would you have done something about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when I took over as commander of the Guards Corps, from Vukovar many envoys were coming with the request, as I have already said, for assistance. At the time, they told me about the highly complicated situation in Vukovar, saying that they were poorly organised, poorly armed, while being surrounded on all sides by JNA units and that from the barracks compound that was situated in Vukovar there was frequent or daily shelling of Vukovar suburbs or, rather, the town of Vukovar. On that occasion, there were expressions of dissatisfaction with the leadership of the Secretariat of National Defence of Vukovar, which was headed at the time by Mercep, the criticism being that he had badly organised things. As for any other knowledge regarding large-scale suffering of any kind is something that I was not aware of at the time, but it should be known that up to 1.200, 1.300 poorly armed men were defending Vukovar, and it would not be logical to assume that they would be able to commit large-scale massacres in relation to the opposing side. Finally, I know that a large number of people of other ethnicities participated in the defence of Vukovar; not just Croats but also Serbs, Hungarians, Slovaks and Czechs. Therefore, it doesn't appear to me to be logical that they could have organised in this way, committed any large-scale massacres. Whether there were individual incidents, that is up to the individuals who have the specific information; I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I want to clarify the situation. Were there reports of casualties at all that were being inflicted on the people of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were. Reports were arriving daily about dead and a large number of wounded that were filling the Vukovar Hospital, and that was the gravest problem, a shortage of medicines and the hospital beds that were overflowing with patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I appreciate that you were not on the spot at the time and you couldn't know from your own direct knowledge, but are you claiming that you know nothing about the killing of several hundred Serb civilians in Vukovar? Is that what you're claiming? Just say yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the barracks in Vukovar was blocked? Just say yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't under blockade. Very well. Tell me then, please -- I should like to move on to a different topic now. Is it true that from the first half of 1992, a large contingent of armed forces from Croatia was situated in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Croatian troops there were in the territory of Odzak municipality in mid-1992? And this is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only comment on the situation regarding the Croatian air force because I was its commander at the time and I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come to that too. And are you familiar with a document of the 14th of June, 1992, in the command of the 2nd HVO Brigade of Odzak municipality to the effect that Serb prisoners from the military prison in Odzak, which was, I assume, under your command, be used to clean minefields, clear minefields, upon which they should be returned to the prison? Did you have occasion to see such an order?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about that, that afterwards they didn't return and so on, so I won't ask you about that. And do you know that according to data of the Yugoslav federal commission for collecting information on war crimes, in Posavina alone in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were 17 camps in which Serbs were detained and that they were under the direct control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about the presence of the Croatian army in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, as the commander of the air defences, you were actively involved in the Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that your activities in connection with Storm were not completed when Knin fell?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The activities ended when the Storm operation ended, and it lasted -- as far as I can remember, it lasted 72 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you monitored the movement of refugee columns containing thousands and thousands of Serbs during that operation, and are you aware of shelling by your air force of those refugee columns?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not know that the Croatian air force shelled refugee columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you lost an officer, a pilot, above the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in those operations against refugee columns. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. During Operation Storm, the Croatian air force did not have a single casualty. It had one plane damaged, which landed at Pleso airport, but not a single human casualty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that for this crime, that is the attack on refugee columns, your former colleague, Croatian Colonel Janko Bobetko, accused you of that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with Janko Bobetko's interview, but as far as I know, he cannot accuse anyone. He can present his position, that is his right, and his opinion. But in those days he was excluded from running the operation, so that he wasn't well-informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what Bobetko said is not true; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to me, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that these are very serious accusations, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were to be true, yes, I agree, they were serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, I assume that all your military archives in Croatia are accessible to you and that as a high-ranking military official, it is easy for you to familiarise yourself with the contents in those archives.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear a question. You were just making a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is, is that true?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I can have access to any document that I ask for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in that context, has anyone from here asked for documents about such serious accusations as those made by Bobetko?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you have the position that you have now, do you believe that there is no problem -- there would be no problems to obtain information from the archives which would disown these accusations of Bobetko's against you, General Tus, Stipetic, and the others? You know that there were various accusations there.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia has committed itself to supply The Hague Tribunal all the documents required by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the Association of Refugees from the Republic of Srpska Krajina, based in Banja Luka, because of these activities, placed you on the list of war crimes responsible for Serb victims in the Storm operation in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but according to the guesswork in some yellow press, I have read that. But officially, I was never informed of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we don't have enough time, I would just like us briefly to cover - very briefly - a few statements contained in the transcript, or the minutes, of the meeting. It says here in the presidential palace on the 23rd of August, 1995, minutes from a conversation between the president, Franjo Tudjman, with military leaders of the Republic of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Croatia, held on the 23rd of August in the presidential palace.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This would be, Mr. May, your 01325991. This is quite a lengthy document, quite lengthy minutes, and I will quote only a couple of passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, it is stated and I quote: "The area of Petrova Gora and around it, in that area before the war, those three municipalities, as seen on this map highlighted in red, was inhabited by 4.259 [as interpreted] Croats, only 4.529 [as interpreted]." I'm quoting this. "And 26.298 Serbs, which means almost virtually vacant area and our national priority number one is to inhabit the area with Croats and to achieve a balance as far as possible." Do you remember that? You attended that meeting, as far as I can see from these minutes.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember attending that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, when the accused has asked his next question about the next passage, you can look at the minutes. You can then tell us about it. Yes, what's your next question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have those minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I know. We'll get them for you. What's the next point, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am just referring here, Mr. May, to a few facts which show that this is actually ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I know. You've made your point. Now, what's the next question? And then the witness can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next question refers to Dr. Jure Radic, who says - this is page 01035995 - in Knin there were 1.600 Croats, in Srb 29, in Doljani not a single one, in Donji Lapac, 14. So these were purely Serb settlements, and this applies in particular to Srb, where there were 29 Croats, in Doljani not a single one, and in Donji Lapac 14. Isn't that right, Mr. Agotic?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were predominantly Serb settlements, but I don't know why I need to comment on that in that connection. I did not attend the meeting at which the ethnic composition was analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was at the meeting that you were present at. I'm only reading from that report, from those minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have a look at the document. Let the witness look at the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have the document. Could Mr. Milosevic be asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No one has the document. Yes. Now, you say he was present at the meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, General, can you tell us if you agree with that or not? Do the minutes show that you were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I have found, Mr. President, I was present. I don't know the details, but judging from what I have found about my own reporting, I stand by what I said today. This is obviously a discussion about the way that Operation Storm should be implemented, which in fact started ten days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And was it -- what was the nature of the meeting? Could you remind us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think there's a misunderstanding here. We're talking about a meeting which, as far as I can understand, was held, as Mr. Milosevic said, on the 23rd of August and not before Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Would you give the witness your copy to make sure we're talking about the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said what it was, but I can't give him a copy. I can give him one later on. All I wish to do is to discuss certain elements from the minutes, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him look at the document which you have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here's the first part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let him look at it and make sure we're talking about the same document. Now, General, is that the same document as the one you've been looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging by the first page, it is, because I've compared the first page. We can compare the third, page 3. Yes, that's page 3. It's the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not to lose more time, Mr. May, if possible. General, take a look at page -- page 01326006. Just a small quotation from that. "I agree that this should be used --" 006, yes, the last digits. That's their number, the one they give us here for the pages to a document. What it says: "I agree that that should be made use of and that in that way we should make Knin Croatian as fast as possible." So this discusses the structure of the population. And then page 00316026 where it says: "Vojnic had 76 Croats and 7.300 Serbs." And then the answer is: "All right. It will be different now." I'm going to skip over the next portion. And here we have something that I've marked to remind you that you were actually there at the meeting. It is page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please read the numbers out more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says Colonel General Migogulz [phoen], these are the two best places for sailing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the page number? Would you read it slowly for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 01326032. And I'm taking this as evidence of the fact that the witness did indeed attend the meeting. It doesn't matter otherwise, he's talking about his own opinions with respect to the airport. But he did attend the meeting, and that's not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you remember the meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember it. It was obviously a meeting that discussed where and how the Croatian army would be deployed on the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to skip over a lot of this material now. Take a look at page 01326073. Tudjman is speaking, and he says, among other things, the middle paragraph on that page: "And then what you said is clear, that we should not be shallow in our thinking. Perhaps somebody saw me and when I said during my last election speech in 1990, I was a little undiplomatic and said that the borders of the -- of Croatian pretzels are untenable, of the Croatian bun are untenable, which means that we did not -- was not by chance that we created the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO and we would have applied these operations there to now. But it means it is true that never in Croatian history did a Croatian soldier control more territory than has been the case hitherto, but it is still clear that in the formal and administrative sense, we cannot have a different organisation than the one we proposed." Therefore, is it possible, General, for you -- that you claim that the Croatian army was not on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it did not take control of the entire area that is being spoken here and the fact that the Croatian soldier never in his entire history held that much territory under his control? And you know that under the NDH there was the whole the Bosnia-Herzegovina that was included --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've stopped -- I've stopped you. You're making a speech. Now, you've read a large section -- you've read a large section of the minutes. Let us begin by saying that. Did President Tudjman, do you remember him saying what he's recorded as saying there? Can you remember that, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember all the details, but there is high probability that the quotation is correct and that that was what was said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I won't go on with that. All I want to do is, in view of the fact that you yourself said that these transcripts -- these minutes are available to you because you are advisor to the present president, so you do have access to them, and so all I wanted to do was to take a look at one of the minutes which related to -- let me just find it, find the portion I'm looking for. And amongst your collaborators and associates or, rather, his, President Tudjman denies stories going round about some sort of meetings that I had. This is on page 01515277 of these minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, is this the same meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, it's not. But this is your number. It took place on the 7th of May in the presidential palace, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 7th of May of which year, so we have it recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1997. 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment while the witness finds it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, just an information. We have these presidential notes, we have then in-house, but we have only translation of parts that actually related to the witness, and those sections that are now quoted from Mr. Milosevic we have not translated here, at least not here in the courtroom, but it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got a copy? We will adjourn so this can be sorted out, but have you got a copy of the 7th of May, 1997?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I assume so but we have not yet found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think the sensible thing would be to adjourn now, it can be found, and we will resume with questioning on it after the adjournment. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've now got copies, as I hope the witness has, of the meeting of the 7th of May in the presidential palace. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you ought to bear in mind that we're progressing fairly slowly, that is to say we're getting through these minutes slowly, so I assume you're going to give me a little more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see how we get on. Let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, first, is it clear what the reason for holding this meeting was? Or, rather, let's put it in a different way: Is it true that with respect to this information meeting which was supplied by, as they say Counsel Nobilo, on the testimony of Stjepan Mesic, that this should remain confidential because they did not want it discovered that this was disclosed about the confidential testimony of Mesic here with respect to something else, another trial.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm looking at this -- these minutes of the 7th of May. First of all, I never attended that meeting. It was with Nenad Ivankovic, Marko Rebic, according to what it says here, the names I can see, Branko Tudjen too, so that I can't tell you any more about that. I would have to read it, study it, and then give you my opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand that. But would you please bear in mind the fact, in view of what you yourself confirmed, that these minutes are available to you, the transcripts of the meetings held by President Tudjman and his associates. Page 015177 [as interpreted], that page, this is what it says, and please listen to this carefully. He says of himself that Tudjman manipulated the situation and used it to his advantage and made decisions which the Sabor or parliament should decide whether the Croatian army should be engaged in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which page is this? Can you help us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 277 [as interpreted]. Page 11 on the minutes themselves page 11. Last digits 277.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "But the essential point is that certain discussions we had are falsely being interpreted. Everything boils down to the fact, and you'll see that I had a meeting with Milosevic 48 times to discuss the division of Bosnia." That's what Tudjman says. And he later on acknowledges that I had a meeting at his proposal for the first time. "I had a meeting with Milosevic twice bilaterally and one together with Alija Izetbegovic, Milosevic and myself, and we even, and you can tell them that --"

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, page 11 and then page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Somewhere in Geneva, he goes on to say. We were together. These things repeated themselves and at the meeting we divided Bosnia and we said that there was never any discussion about the division of Bosnia, the carving up in Bosnia. But with Alija in the spring of 1992, we did discuss this. Alija -- the war was stopped, but Alija wanted to remain in Yugoslavia. And then he goes on to say that a solution was that a Serbo-Croatian meeting was reached to put an end to the war. Now, is it clear, according to all this, that your former boss Mesic testified falsely about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm not going to admit this. The witness was not there. It's quite impossible for him to comment on something else when he wasn't present. Now, there's no point asking him, particularly asking him to comment on some other witness's testimony. You can ask him, of course, about meetings at which he was present, but the status of these minutes of meetings at which he was not present is something we'll have to consider, and certainly that question is one which he cannot possibly answer. Yes. Have you any more questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I bore in mind, Mr. May, the fact that the general does have access to all these minutes and that he was able to establish what President Tudjman is saying here, to establish the correctness of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The fact that he's got access to the minutes does not mean that he can give evidence about them. Of course if he's present that's one thing, but if not, it's quite impossible for him to comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Mr. May. I take it I can't ask him anything about the minutes. But I assume that we can observe that this is the original document, the original minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it look authentic to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does look authentic. And if the Croatian side disclosed it officially, then there's no reason to doubt it, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, General, your former superior, General Anton Tus, was the head of the standing mission of -- to NATO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, General, the Croatian air force under your command was not only active during Operation Storm but previously as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that the Croatian air force, following orders from you, became involved in the airspace above Bosnia-Herzegovina and took part there together with the Muslim forces in an operation against the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean acted and took part in together with? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the form of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true that it participated in combat activities together with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it didn't bomb and shell the columns of Bosnian Serbs or their positions. It did not bomb this -- the forces of the Bosnian Serbs for the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not bomb on the side of the Muslim side, nor did it engage in any combat activity in the territory of Bosnia except for 1992, I believe, or perhaps 1993, I don't remember exactly. To the south of the Sava River, towards the artillery positions there, from which the settlements were being targeted on the left bank of the Sava River on Croatian territory, in fact. So on that occasion, one MiG 21 plane was shot down and the pilot killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the pilot's name?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pilot's name was Anton Rados.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you use a pilot by the name of Perisin or something similar?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you lose this other pilot in the airspace above Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perisin was shot down on the territory of the Republic of Croatia in the course of the -- of Operation Flash, on the 2nd of May, 1995. And his plane to this day lies on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. It was not pulled out of the area, it lies there still, and that is material proof that he was knocked down over Croatian airspace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A part of the plane fell on the territory of Croatia and another part on Republika Srpska. And did you find Perisin there?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know -- as far as we know as to the spot the plane fell on, and he fell on actually because he was catapulted out of the plane, it was on the south bank of the Sava River. That means in Bosnia. He was catapulted from Bosnia but the plane actually crashed down on the left bank of the Sava River, which means on Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, so the plane fell on Croatia and he fell in Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He fell on the bent embankment. He was captured or, rather, killed, or perhaps he had already been killed as he was falling to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know any precise details about that but it was in operations against the Serb forces, without a doubt?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Against the forces not of Republika Srpska but against the forces of the so-called army of SAO Krajina, on the left bank of the Sava River before you get to the bridge at Stare Gradiska. He was given an assignment to hit the artillery positions which were defending the bridge and targeting Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, General.
