Now, tell me this, please: Do you know the contents of the piece of information by the security department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna dated the 14th of September, 1993, that is to say, the time when the Croatian forces could not have been present on the territory at all?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read something out to you - I have the document in front of me - and then I'm going to let you have a look at it. And from the document you can see it says: "As from Vitez an appeal was launched about the critical situation with regard to ammunition, we undertook to realise the -- to take steps in this matter." And then it says that a helicopter at Lovric from the headquarters of the HVO was asked to table a request for Divulje, that is to say for your own base there, that it has three seriously wounded men in Vitez and that they had to ensure helicopter transport to evacuate them. This was after the talk with Mr. Agotic, and he said let the wounded people go to Kiseljak, be taken to Kiseljak, like the other ones from Nova Bila, which means this was a code name, there were no wounded and injured persons, what you were actually doing was transporting ammunition, and that can be seen from this letter. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war in Bosnia, Croatia used a transport helicopter to perform more than 100 flights with the aim of evacuating the wounded and injured from the Nova Bila area as well as Kiseljak, Vares and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand all that, General, but here it says quite openly that Kiseljak, Medjugorje, that an operation was there, and General Agotic took advantage of the occasion to give us this explanation as if he didn't know the background of activities of that kind. And then it goes on to state we flew at an altitude of such-and-such. We landed successfully at the exit to Busovaca, and without switching off our engines, we started unloading the ammunition. So there's no question of any wounded persons. The unloading lasted about eight minutes after which we flew off again and successfully arrived at Firule and after at Divulje. As the place of unloading in Busovaca, there was no -- there were no wounded persons there, we didn't take anybody with us, and we explained to the EEC monitors that we were targeted while we were landing and so we gave up the idea, and they accepted that explanation with all seriousness. So there's no evacuation of wounded here. What this was about was an ammunitions transport. You can take a look at the document yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see the document. Just a moment. Let him have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the document -- community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, would you first of all tell us what the date of the document is, please, if you can see one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 14th of September, 1993. They are the same documents, both. Mr. President, I see this document for the first time. I don't know whether it is authentic. I cannot vouch for that. And it is difficult for me, therefore, to comment all that it contains. But at Firule if the helicopter landed at Firule, then it brought the wounded. Otherwise, there was no need for it to land at Firule. So there must have been wounded, because he's reporting that he landed at Firule in Split. Now, whether in the course of these sorties which were engaged in in order to evacuate the wounded and the injured and the delivery of medicines to the hospital in Nova Bila where there was a hospital all the time throughout the war and took some other type of aid, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. Nova Bila, remind me, is that near Vitez, or where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. Nova Bila is in Vitez municipality. It was a wartime hospital there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it's accepted that there were helicopter flights in order to evacuate the wounded from there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were more than a hundred flights to evacuate the wounded and injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance. This document was translated by the OTP. We have it in English too. I received it the other day from the OTP. So I would like to ask them to supply you with a copy. It is in English, the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm claiming quite the opposite; that this was not evacuation of wounded, as you explained the second paragraph of this report: "It should be noted that the Kiseljak Medjugorje operation was ongoing which General Agotic took advantage of to provide such an explanation as if he was unaware of the background of these activities."

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I repeat that I do not know whether the document is authentic. I'm just claiming that transport unarmed helicopters were used to evacuate more than a thousand wounded and injured from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, all parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. So you're claiming that you did not deliver ammunition to your forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina in this way. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my responsibility nor did I have any control over the ammunition, and that is what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming that helicopters under your command were not used to transport ammunition.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am claiming that they were not used under my command for the transport of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. May, I should like to tender this into evidence. Now, whether it is authentic or not is easy to establish. Also, I would like to tender the first minutes of the meeting that was attended by General Agotic. The first minutes, not the second one which you say he is unable to comment on but the first one at which he did attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's unable to comment on it, but on the other hand, he recognised it as authentic and therefore we may well be able to exhibit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first document that Mr. Milosevic wants to be exhibited is the one from the 23rd of August, 1995, and Mr. Agotic was present during these -- this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first set of minutes, which is the 23rd of August, 1995, will be given the first Defence Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 153, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next minutes, those of the 7th of May, although it's right the witness wasn't present, nonetheless, he has stated its authenticity and we admit such documents, can be given the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 154, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And finally, the Herceg-Bosna document of the 14th of September, 1993, that can have the final Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you had occasion, Mr. Agotic, to see a statement? I have only received it only in English, by Arif Pasalic, a statement he made here which is very lengthy, and almost entirely it is devoted to the involvement of Croatian forces in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have occasion to see his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you like to have a look at it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, it's what somebody else said, and it's totally irrelevant as far as this witness is concerned. If you want to put something from it to the witness, you can, but there's no point the witness looking at it, and it's not admissible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I could present the whole statement to him, but, for instance, on page 7 of that statement it says: "On the 26th of October, 1992, I arrived in Prozor [In English] and General Slobodan Praljak who was a general of the Croatian army, but he was in the HVO HQ - HVO headquarters - and also with us was Pero Zelenika of the HVO and Srecko Vucina of the HVO headquarters main staff Mostar. The units of HVO, some of whom had the insignia of the Croatian army and the commander of the unit Siljeg, who I think at the time had the rank of major now controlled Prozor."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is the 26th of October, 1992. Was General Slobodan Praljak a general of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, by then he was already a general of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was a Croatian general doing in Prozor if you say that the Croatian army was not in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina during those operations?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in command of General Praljak. He was in the Defence Ministry, assistant minister for political work?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this statement be -- Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We were discussing, Mr. Milosevic, how much longer you should have, and we've decided that you should have an extra 15 minutes. That gives you 20 minutes in all. Now, yes. No. If you want the statement exhibited, you know the answer is no. You've applied often enough before. Statements of witnesses are not admissible unless there are exceptional circumstances, which don't apply here. You can always call this witness, if you want. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this particular detail that I quoted from the statement, would you like to comment on it or not? Do you believe it to be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But let us conclude on this point. You said very clearly that the Croatian army, during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's fine. Allow me now to go back to a matter, because you said that while Vasiljevic was head of security in the JNA or, rather, the security administration of the JNA, there were no members of other ethnicities, is it true that the security administration always had two generals, and as a rule they were Croats? There was Miskovic, Domankusic, who is Mrs. Florence Hartmann's father-in-law. Grubisic, Paricevic, Pavicic. Were they all in the security administration and were they all Croats?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were generals in the security administration. I don't know the ethnicity of all of them. This was a long time ago, and in those days I didn't give that any thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is alleged that one of them is Mrs. Florence Hartmann's father-in-law. Do you know if that's so or not? You may not know who Mrs. Florence Hartmann is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mrs. Florence Hartmann when she's making statements on Croatian television. Now, whether she's married and what her family background is, I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When General Vasiljevic was head of the administration, his deputy was General Tumanov, who was a Macedonian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Head of the first department, a Slovene, a colonel, Maks Pen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was head of the first department at that time, but I do know that Maks Pen is a Slovene and that for a time he was in the security service. Now, what position he held after 1989, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then a Croat, Lorenzini, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know him while he was serving in the 5th Military District. Now, what position he held after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that while -- at the time that you were suspended, you were suspected of having connections with the foreign intelligence service, and there was a danger of you being taken to court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. In your examination-in-chief, you referred to certain events, and tab 34 was used as an example, a report by a major. I haven't noted his name properly, I think it's Riksic or something like Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that, about the suffering of civilians in Skabrnja. And this was addressed to the 9th Corps, as you explained it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then in tab 35, the report of the commander of the military police platoon, also from Skabrnja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear from this that -- that there was an investigation with respect to the activities engaged in by representatives of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is my assessment, that security organs of the military police conducted an investigation into the situation in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You heard, and I think you used an example, tab 5, for the events in Fruska. The explanation given was that an Ustasha sabotage terrorist group was involved. You heard and you claim that this was attributed to Croats but that the JNA had a different position than the one presented by the police in Benkovac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean, according to tab 6, that the JNA conducted its investigation in an unbiased manner, according to what you say?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to that report, that is the right conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you went on to speak about - and this is in tab 7 - about the arrival of 24 people from Knin. And from what you commented on professionally, you said they were people from SAO Krajina and not the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had urged that the newly elected leaderships of Slovenia and Croatia needed to be recognised. I have to tell you, General, that I hear from you for the first time that the leaderships of Slovenia and Croatia were not recognised, that they were unrecognised. Do you remember that those leaderships participated in regular political life of Yugoslavia, that the president attended meetings of the Presidency of the SFRY when presidents of the republics were invited? I personally attended many sessions together with Tudjman and the others, other members of the Presidency of the SFRY, and he attended as president of Croatia and I as president of Serbia. So what kind of lack of recognition are you referring to regarding the leaderships of Slovenia and Croatia? Janez Stanovnik from Slovenia was also present.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement, Mr. Milosevic, related to recognition of the top of the JNA leadership of the new leaderships.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're talking about the JNA attitudes.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I gave an example to illustrate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Let us clear up just one more detail. You said that you were the authorised negotiator with the JNA, that on behalf of the JNA there was General Raseta, who most frequently consulted with Admiral Brovet. That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Admiral Brovet at the time was Deputy Federal Secretary for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Admiral Brovet is a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is generally thought that he was a Slovenian. Now, whether he considers himself that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: His name is Stane Brovet, so I think that is quite clearly a Slovenian first and last name. But no one ever doubted that he was a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I think too, but it's his right to declare himself as he will, so I haven't seen his declaration of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were asked something with respect to these negotiations with Raseta, whether people were leaving of their own free will, and your response to that was that there was general practice in those parts that they would come individually or in groups and cross over into the territory under the control of the Croatian authorities. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they were driven into the separation line by the authorities of the SAO Krajina of the day. Yes, it's true. They came as individuals and in groups too, they would come to the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you explained that people fled in the face of combat operations too, in the face of the fighting, that they left the area, as you yourself said, faced with the front. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was that a form of ethnic cleansing then or was it just fleeing from the fighting?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the occupation of the territory, we can say the people fled in the face of the fighting, but a planned intimidation through artillery shelling also took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was -- they planned to instil fear into the people so that they should leave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And does that apply to Operation Storm when Knin was shelled and when the citizens left the area en masse?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the Storm operation, it was military targets that were targeted and shelled. And as far as I know, this is always done in order to diminish the army's ability to defend itself and not to have the population leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the people that stayed on were later on slaughtered and killed. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about data of that kind, but I assume there were cases of retaliation and revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me about this: You mentioned Saborsko and November 1991. Is it, however, true that it was following your orders that an attack had been launched previously on the strategic ammunitions depot belonging to the JNA which was located near Saborsko and in Licka Jesenica? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that there was a depot there or that I issued orders to that effect, along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You don't remember. But can I jog your memory that Colonel Bulat, via a mediator in the European Union, sent you an appeal to stop the attack but that you intensified the attack after that and that the attack on the depot reached a crux on the 12th of November, 1991, that it culminated on that date?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that that's how it was, but I don't remember those details. And as regards Saborsko, I just commented on the map that was shown to me and gave my opinions about the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you gave your opinions as to the map. I see. From your professional viewpoint. You didn't present the data that you knew about. You were just commenting on the map, were you?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was commenting on the map and also I said that Saborsko was cleansed and what partially led up to that from talks with the mayor or head of the municipality before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said, actually, that the president of the local community of Saborsko reported and asked you to arm them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And his name was Luka Hodak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then later on you went on to say that the citizens fled prior to the conflict and that the defenders, as you called them, withdrew in the face of a stronger force. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So were there any crimes that were committed against the population at the time or was it a purely military operation?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite obviously a military operation. Now, whether in the course of that military operation any crimes took place as well, I don't know. But a crime is a crime if you want to leave the village empty of its inhabitants so that you could go ahead and destroy the village after that. So that is, for me, a crime and the inordinate use of force along with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: As there was fighting that culminated on the 12th of November, 1991, fighting around this depot, do you remember that it was under your command that some foreign mercenaries fought? There were Scandinavians, for example, and among the dead on your side there were several people who quite obviously were not from the Yugoslav parts. The colour of their skin was different and they were also foreign mercenaries. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Croatian army there were dozens of nationalities and foreign nationals, in fact. I don't know the exact figure, and I don't know who they were and who died where, but many of them were killed, that is true. They were not foreign mercenaries who were engaged in the pejorative sense, they were volunteers who had come up to join the ranks of the regular Croatian army of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, General. Now, as you say you commented on the map and the 5th Partisan Brigade was mentioned, do you happen to know that in Saborsko and the surrounding parts, at least according to the information that I have been given, collected by my associates, that there was no 5th Partisan Brigade of any kind? It was the 9th Light Brigade from Licka Jesenica, in fact, which was there and which, in fact, deblocked the kerosine and ammunitions depot there.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the possibility that the 9th Light Brigade was used to that effect because there were quite a number of units in the area. However, it was the Partisan -- whether it was the 5th Partisan or some other title, some other name, it was responsible for that territory. Now, what the make-up was in the former JNA and how it became part of the SAO Krajina army...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, let's just go back for a moment to a question we were discussing, and we cleared it up. It wasn't that there was no recognition of Croatia and Slovenia because they took part normally and then you reduced this to meaning the JNA, to refer to the JNA alone. Now, my information tells me that there is television footage from the first Sabor of the newly elected leadership with the presence of representatives of the JNA there as guests. They were guests invited. They were representatives of the JNA, the command in charge of Croatia, and so on.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of this footage, so I can't comment. But what I do know is that JNA representatives from the corresponding commands and headquarters did attend the constituting of the first Sabor parliament of the Republic of Croatia once the new authorities had come into power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were present. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when the Croatian Assembly was constituted, known as the Sabor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when the newly elected president was promoted, President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the JNA didn't boycott the new authorities, did it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was the JNA, but what I do know is that there was a commander there of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia. He was present. And there is a picture of him in the Croatian parliament to this day. But I don't remember who was present on the JNA side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that a company of the Territorial Defence from Plasko was at Saborsko; right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Plasko, yes, there was one. And it took some sort of part in the operation on Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you emphasise that it wasn't an operation launched by the Territorial Defence but the lawful and -- of the lawful and legitimate JNA units; right? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an operation both on the part of the Serbian Territorial Defence along with participation of JNA units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is now up. You can ask one more question, though, of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as you said, General, that a part of the weaponry was destroyed, could you please comment on these facts and figures that I have been given. We refer to Delnice and Grobnicko Polje and the warehouse or depot in Sapijane, if I've got the name right. Is it true and correct that the attack by the ZNG on the 11th of October, 1991, the Croatian National Guard Corps was launched against the warehouse of the 5th Military District, its depot, and that the defence was put up by a unit of the Delnice Brigade, commander of the Viljeka Corps, under the command of Colonel Dzuro Vitanovic, and that the fighting went on until the 15th of October to secure control and that finally the depot was taken over on the 17th of October and that the JNA did not set fire to anything, that you were able to take on the entire contents, although prior to that an agreement had been reached with you about a non-attack, a non-attack agreement. And at the head of the Croatian National Guard Corps was Colonel Jokovic who was expelled from the JNA, and then later on, you expelled him too, after an abortive attack on a village in Lika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us restrict this to one question. The question that you can ask is this: General, would you deal with the allegation concerning an attack in October on the warehouse of the 5th Military District. Is the account which the accused has given of that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just finish my sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was a warehouse that was guarded by 70 soldiers and the attack was launched by 2.000 members of the Croatian National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the ratio -- I can't say what the ratio of forces was but that we had 2.000 members of the ZNGs in the Delnice region, had we had that number, then we would have done the job far quicker. So I doubt as to the correctness of those figures. However, taking control of the warehouse in Delnice did take place, perhaps on the date that Mr. Milosevic states, and after that, and that was customary generally speaking, two days later in fact, the warehouse was bombed by the JNA air force and everything destroyed, everything that was not pulled out was destroyed, and that was the principle followed in all the activities when warehouses were taken over by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, you've had your time. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Agotic, yesterday during the examination-in-chief you spoke about some documents which are contained in the list of exhibits that attended your testimony, and you mentioned some of them in the various tabs. And for Sabici and some other documents, when you looked at them in view of their contents, formed the way in which they were compiled, you said that they were authentic documents. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you said about Sabici? Which Sabic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There were several documents whose authenticity you confirmed.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Even some documents that weren't signed you said you thought were authentic ones.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because that's how they were written during my time in the JNA. They didn't need to contain signatures and they were considered authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, this document, the one that was shown to you a moment ago, dated the 14th of September, 1993, when you yourself were already a member of the Croatian army. I should like to ask you now to take a look at that document. I have a copy here. I don't know if it's been given back to you. Do you have a copy? No? Here it is, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document has been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's Defence Exhibit 155.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the document, you'll be able to see that it has a number and a date. It says "Memorandum" and it has a stamp in the upper Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. right-hand corner, and it even has some initials at the bottom. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp is illegible so I can't guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but everything else, judging by the form, how it was compiled, was compiled in the way that these things were done when you were commander of the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any rules as to how documents should be written in the intelligence service and security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand that. But I'd like to ask you whether you know what this at the bottom might mean, the initials BA. Who could that be?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually they are the initials of the man who compiled the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you to focus on the contents, and they mention these flights and that President Tudjman was consulted with respect to those flights. Is that right? Do you know that President Tudjman was consulted with respect to those flights?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't consulted for each individual flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, can you tell me who Colonel Ticinovic is?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Ticinovic was the commander of the air force base of Divulje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And he was under your command?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 5 -- one, two, three, four -- paragraph 4, several hours -- after several hours of indecision, General Pupotic [phoen], Nagotic [phoen] gave their permission for the flight, a flight that transported 190.000 pieces of ammunition, 7.62 calibre. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the customary procedure for giving the okay for the flights. Now, what the contents were, what the cargo was, I can't say for sure, whether the planes contained what you say they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But take a look at the document. We see that permission was asked by the ECMMs, that first of all they did not give their permission for the flight and then after Bagaric's report was received that they were dealing with three soldiers who were in a coma, that permission was given for the flight. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was customary. Dr. Bagaric was the head of the medical corps of the Croatian Defence Council, as far as I remember, or rather, the head of the hospital in Novo Bila and Kiseljak, thereabouts, in those parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now take a look at paragraph 2 on page 2, and it says the following -- is it true? That the European Community was explained that we were targeted in our attempts to land and that we gave up the idea; that is to say that we never went through with it. They never went through with it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything that can be brought into dispute there. They accepted that with all seriousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And finally, it says this flight caused a wave of enthusiasm once again in the population and the soldiers and as is characteristic after flights of this kind, an operation is launched to cleanse part of the territory taken control of. For example, Grbavica was cleansed. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you something else, something about the minutes. One of the minutes was presented here to this Trial Chamber a few days ago, and it has to do with the meeting on the 31st of July held on Brioni islands in 1995. Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did attend one meeting. Now, whether that was that particular meeting I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll ask you something about that later on. And the other was held on the 23rd of August, 1995, and you've already said that you did attend that particular meeting. Will you now take a look, please, at page 21 on the B/C/S version or, rather, it is the -- the number is -- the ERN number is 26011. I have it here. I have a copy here, in fact. Could you have a look at page 26011. And what Major General Vinko Vrbanjac says. Have you got it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what he says: "Mr. President, by liberating the third part of the occupied territory, the Republic of Croatia has created the conditions for what you said in your introduction to in a military fashion in fact arrive at a change in the population." Is that what he said? Did he say that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then afterwards, the president says the following: "It is by a lucky chance that this liberation in view of the strategic position in fact requires a deployment of our military units which would solve to a great extent the demographic setup." Did you hear that? Did you hear him say that? Was it what he said and can you comment, please.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These matters were discussed probably at that meeting as well, but this has to do with something quite different, Mr. Tapuskovic; namely, after the war, it was felt that Croatia should devote more attention to certain neglected areas by refreshing them demographically by stationing the army in those areas, and the discussion was to that effect rather than the army going there and chasing out a population of a different ethnicity from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Now, look at page 26067, I think it's towards the end in the B/C/S version, where President Tudjman is speaking. The same document. The number is 01326067. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to quote just a part of it. You can comment on it, but I'm only interested in this point. He started in this way wait: "Wait, wait, let us be realistic now," and then look at the end. True, this is reference to Vitalina and Molunat - two letters are missing - but it says: "We had half a million Serbs there and where are they now?" Do you remember this being said? We had half a million Serbs, and where are they now?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference is probably to the entire territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now, are you familiar with a report, because you say that the whole Operation Storm was completed 72 -- after 72 hours, and after that there was no threat to the safety of people, to their property and their lives. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the operation was completed in that time and that the Croatian army had completed its part of the work. It had liberated the area. As for the establishment of authorities, that is up to someone else, not the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have a document which I received from the OTP. Their Honours can look at it. I have sufficient number of copies. This is document Weekly Assessment of the Command of the ECMM in Zagreb of the 14th of August, 1995, number 2668536858. And it says on page 3: "Five weeks after Operation Storm, harassment continued and in some cases killing of Serb inhabitants, which means several weeks after the Croatian forces had been deployed in the area. So killings continued as well as constant looting, which is contrary to official reports according to which law and order had been established. In fact, this is continuing because of lack of interest on the part of the Croatian government to put an end to it." Are you familiar with this report of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I must ask you how you see your role. I mean, this seems to be just repeating what the accused is saying. You're not here to represent Serbia, you're here to assist the Court. The accused is putting forward a defence, and there's no reason for you to add to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really am not at all trying to be a Defence counsel for Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. I am trying to act in accordance with your instructions, to draw your attention to every matter which I consider to be important for you. I am focusing only on documents. I haven't tendered a single document myself. I am only focusing on the documents I received from the OTP and drawing your attention to them. I'm not trying to defend anyone, I'm just highlighting matters about which it is up to you to rule. We have a witness here that you will believe or you will not believe, that is absolutely up to you. But it is my duty to draw your attention to documents that I believe you need to devote your attention to, and that is all I am doing. I think they are important, and I think that when you have to determine -- make your determinations, that you need to bear them in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything you want to say about it, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, would you please repeat to me what is the date of that ECMM report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is a report of the ECMM of the 14th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This was ten days after the operation.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said five weeks after the Operation Storm that massacres continued, and on the 14th of August, that was only nine days after the beginning of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you said that everything was over in 72 hours.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am claiming that the military part of the operation was completed in 72 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I won't go back to that again, but let me also draw the attention of Their Honours to one further point. Do you remember attending a meeting on the 31st of July, 1995, when the last words by President Tudjman were the following: "Wait. I'm going to Geneva in order to conceal this and not to discuss things there. I will not send a minister, I will send the Assistant Minister of Internal Affairs to conceal what we are preparing for the day after so that we eliminate all arguments to the world that we didn't wish to negotiate but we wished only," et cetera. Do you remember President Tudjman saying that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended the meeting at Brioni just prior to Operation Storm. I do not recollect that particular detail. But do you think that someone would publish, would announce to the whole world that they were engaging in an operation, about to engage in an operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not claiming anything, Mr. Agotic, I'm just drawing attention to what was said. And here are some more words by the president: "But I am mentioning this because we must conceive our operations and implement them in such a way not to give cause to Yugoslavia, Milosevic, and their friends in the West to accept the intervention of Yugoslavia on Croatian soil." End of quote. Do you remember that that was what was said? And then he repeated again, "I'm saying again, we must not left ourselves be provoked so as to give Yugoslavia a cause to go to war." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, on that same page, it says: "Next year we will have Croatia and tourism, and also we will be shaping the borders of Croatia in Bosnia." This was stated in 1995. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular detail regarding Bosnia but that we had extra forces that could be reduced, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we have the minutes from the 23rd of August that you attended. Do you remember that the president said the following on that occasion: "If international circumstances were such, and if we had had the wisdom, and if I had been told that the Yugoslav air force, assisted with Russian rockets, would be engaged in this war, then today we would have had borders that would have suited not only Croatia but the whole world"?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that probably the entire minutes are authentic, but that particular detail, in view of the time distance and the length of the meeting, I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer my question if there was fear that the Yugoslav army would get involved? That means that in the Serbian Krajina, where the operation was conducted -- not Serbian Krajina, in the Krajina inhabited by Serbs, there was no Yugoslav army at the time.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But then in Croatia, there were no Yugoslav army forces.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was no longer called the Yugoslav army, it was called the army of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And let me complete this questioning with the minutes. If you could please look at the last page or, rather, I'll read it out to you, the last page of this report of the 23rd of August, 1995, in which it says as follows, the very end: "Then it's not a tactical matter. It is a matter for state policies, and does my word mean anything?" And then what I think to be particularly important: "For me to be able to rely on allies and friends who, as you can see, are such that they are not pursuing our policies but their own policies." End of quote. Does that really mean that the friends he's referring to here were more concerned about their own strategic and political goals than the interests of Croatia, as President Tudjman put it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only logical that everyone should give priority to one's own interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As I don't have much time, finally let me ask you one more thing. Since between 1971 and 1974, you were in Bihac working in security affairs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember events linked to the Croatian spring?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The mass movement.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is true that that was the first major separatist, nationalist action designed to achieve Croatia's independence?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not right. It was a movement in Croatia which set out requests for redefining internal relationships within the former Yugoslavia, which was a perfectly legal requirement of one of the members of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But wasn't that movement halted precisely because the JNA, under the leadership of Josip Broz Tito, was still very powerful?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And the international circumstances were such that it was halted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I probably wouldn't have asked you this had you not worked in the area. Bugojno was within your area of responsibility, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. I didn't have a particular territory. There our ground forces held the territory, not the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that a very large terrorist group was infiltrated at the time whose aim was to start an uprising, and there was a serious conflict between the JNA and that group?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with that case and the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, do I have a few more minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, just a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The ideas of the Croatian spring, were they reflected when the constitution was adopted in 1974 when eight states were formed and the JNA was broken up as a basis for some future activities?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the victories of the so-called Croatian spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me now, when President Mesic testified here - and it can also be found in Kucan's statement, although I didn't have time to question him about it - that there were three integrating factors of the unity of Yugoslavia: First, the authority of Josip Broz Tito; secondly, the League of Communists; and thirdly, the powerful Yugoslav People's Army. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of that statement, and I agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: With the death of Josip Broz Tito, the first condition was available for achieving disintegration, and were certain activities engaged in already in 1980 after his death? And I'm sure that you had intelligence information already then that could be used for the break-up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there were individuals who wanted the break-up of Yugoslavia, but when I speak about the disappearance of three integrating factors for Yugoslavia, I am thinking of the Yugoslavia that we had up until then. It needed to be redefined, and this required the political will of all parties. Yes. Tito had physically gone, but his authority still lasted.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then that authority had to be undermined too.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people wanted to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And wasn't that done when his birthday ceased to be celebrated, then abolishing the relay baton race that existed regularly for his birthday, and finally, the military parade on the 9th of May in observation of Victory Day was no longer held. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did the League of Communists need to be broken up?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If was one of the integrating factors. It needed to be redefined. That's how I see the 14th Congress.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And was the main principle of the League of Communists democratic centralism, which meant that until a decision is taken, everyone can have his own opinion, but afterwards, the majority opinion should prevail?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not non-democratic centralism, which would mean outvoting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've really heard this, thank you very much. Anything more you want to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll go directly to a question and the point of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As you worked in the intelligence and security service, did you know, and we heard from somebody who was your superior, Mr. Vasiljevic, but had you heard of the existence of two plans, that first every attempt be made either to provoke the JNA so that it should started acting first, or to attack the JNA? Provoke it or attack it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who had such plans?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Had you heard of any such plans from within certain circles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the point: You're now putting forward a positive Defence case, and it's not your role, in my judgement, to do that. The accused does that. Now, unless there's anything more, I think we need to go on to the re-examination in order to finish by quarter past.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll finish my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you were speaking about the capture of barracks, did this occur in the second half of August before any conflict of any scale had started?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the second half of August when the main operation started to capture barracks and block them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of July, you virtually stopped working in the JNA, and is it true that on the 1st of July, Mr. Mesic became president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date when he became president.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber the following: When what happened happened, you said that the Yugoslav army became a Serbian army. Roughly, something to that effect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And all officers and soldiers who were Croats, did they all remain in the Croatian army, the others in the Bosnian army or in the Macedonian army? Virtually when the Yugoslav People's Army broke up, several new armies were formed, and they inherited a certain portion of the weaponry of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partially true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic. Mr. Tapuskovic, because since you are a legal expert, being different from the accused, I'd like to ask this question. You dealt with some -- Operation Storm and some later events afterwards which took place much after the events which -- which is included in the indictment against the accused. What I would like to ask you is this: What relevance does it have in relation to the indictment? Could you explain it in legal terms? Is it a self-defence or are you triggering a tu quoque theory, or what else?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you will be ruling about that. It is my duty to address all matters which might be of significance for your determination. In my judgement as an amicus, it is my opinion that all the circumstances that preceded all these events need to be studied carefully. This is a rare case in the history of civilisation that an army within a territory on one day -- these are people who served in the army from Serbia, in Slovenia, people from Montenegro and Kosovo. This was all a mixture, a melting pot. In a single day, this ceased to be the Yugoslav People's Army, and you need to examine the circumstances in which that Yugoslav People's Army broke up, disappeared from the stage, and how all this affected the behaviour of the people who constituted that state. It is very difficult to determine the actual turning point when this happened, and this state of mind among the people when a state disappeared in one moment. Therefore, you need to establish that there were plans for criminal action. It is up to you to determine this, of course. I am confident, and that is why I am addressing these matters, that at that point in time there were no plans to engage in crime, that this was initially a civil war and that mostly it was a civil war, and as amicus curiae, we have presented our views in our submissions prior to Croatia, the Croatian case, and I think it is up to you in the first place to decide whether a civil war broke out first and then was followed by all these events that you have to adjudicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I asked about is the Operation Storm. I think there's a point in what you are saying, but what significance does it have in relation to legal terms? Because you are a friend of the court and a legal expert - we are not in a history class - what does it have to do with the indictment? Could you spell it out specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honours. It is up to you to rule on the legal matters, whether this was the right to self-defence in all the areas in which this happened. Storm is a consequence of what the Serb population in Krajina feared. It is what caused the things we are talking about. So this problem, this right to self-determination, is another important issue that you will have to rule on. But of course, I believe that in that context, you will need to bear in mind certain historical facts, because unless you as Judges do not delve into those historical circumstances to some extent, I fear that you would be seriously amiss. Not going back I don't know how long into history but at least covering the Second World War period. And unless those things are taken into consideration, I think that would be a very serious omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's all. I can get as much as I can now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Two quick questions. The first relates to the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic put to you whether these barracks were blocked, and your answer to this was no. And I would like to clarify about which time period you were actually speaking. Were the Vukovar barracks ever blocked by the Croats, and if so, was it deblockaded at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks at Vukovar were never under the blockade of the Croatian forces, and on a regular basis, people could go in and out of it onto the side controlled by the Territorial Defence of the day, of Serbia, or, rather, the Serb part of the population south of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the second question I have relates to the Operation Storm. General, did the Croatian army have any intelligence on the possible reactions of the FRY or the VJ before launching the operation?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have intelligence data available to me of that kind which would indicate the reactions of Yugoslavia and what it would be. They were just assessments, that the possibility existed, et cetera, et cetera, that from the area of Serbia, from Yugoslavia, actually, that there would be reactions in a certain way through some breakthroughs onto the territory of the Republic of Croatia from the eastern sector, Sector East, that is to say the eastern zone which was occupied at the time. I'm referring to the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General Agotic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. One matter was raised. It doesn't concern the witness at all, it's to do with the exhibits, so you don't have to be concerned. I'm told there's no difficulty about the exhibits, in fact. But there is one matter I want to raise. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you had put in a motion for four Croatian 92 bis witnesses to be introduced. I guess you're dealing with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient if we hear briefly about it tomorrow before the adjournment, so at about half past one tomorrow, if you'd like to be in then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will be tendering a binder of 16 exhibits. Could I ask that that binder be assigned a number at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's Prosecution Exhibit 476.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we could begin the examination with the witness being shown Prosecution Exhibit 476, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you to look at the top line of this exhibit and ask you if that's your name contained therein.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For the purposes of protecting your identity, you will be referred to as B-1244.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that under seal and ask that we go into closed session briefly for a related matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to begin your testimony by identifying, with a sentence or two, several people. I'm also going to display on the television screen before you a chart, and I would ask you, have you seen this chart that's displayed on the television screen before today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought to have his pseudonym for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness will be testifying under the pseudonym B-1244.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Displayed on the screen is Prosecution Exhibit 476, tab 4. Have you seen this exhibit before today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will not ask you to describe in any great detail the exhibit at this juncture. I will ask you at the conclusion of your testimony to describe what the different boxes and lines indicate, but I will ask that it be displayed while I ask you to give us some information about particular individuals. The first person I would ask you to tell us in a sentence or two who he was is a person by the name of Dragan Djordjevic, also known as Crni.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, was a member of the Serbian Radical Party and also a member of the special units of the DB, the state security, and for a time he was a brigade commander as well in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next person is Srecko Radanovic, also known as Debeli.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: He was also a member of the Radical Party. He was in a group which arrived to the area, and for a time he acted as Chief of Staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, just going to Crni for a second, you've testified that he was a member of the special units of the DB of the state security. Can you be more specific about which state security service he was a member of.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Well, the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Debeli, what was his command relationship with respect to Mr. Crni?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, he occupied a lower post, a lower-ranking post than this man Djordjevic. He was below him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you to tell us in a sentence or two who was Slobodan Miljkovic, also known as Lugar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: He was also a member of the Radical Party, and he arrived in the unit. He was a member of that special unit and the leader of a group within the special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say "special unit," can you tell us precisely what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: I'm referring to the special unit of the state security of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Frenki Simatovic, can you tell us who he was in a sentence or two.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: He was the assistant to the chief of the state security department and commander of that special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic was the chief of the state security service of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Milos Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Milos Bogdanovic was the head of the municipal Secretariat of the National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for which area was he the Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: For the area of -- actually, for mobilisation and sending recruits to do their military service. I think that was his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How large was his area of responsibility? Was it a single municipality or was it larger than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Well, before 1992, he was just there for one municipality. However, at the beginning of 1992, he was also in charge of the newly established Serbian municipality. He was the head there, and that incorporated parts of the other three municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Chamber has heard quite a bit of evidence about a Radmilo Bogdanovic. These two Bogdanovics are not related, according to information you have, are they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, they're not related.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us who a person by the name of Blagoje Simic is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, and during the war he was the head or, rather, president of the Crisis Staff of that same municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Simo Zaric was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Simo Zaric had a number of functions. Before the war, he was head of the state security department for the region. At the beginning of 1992, he was the assistant commander for a security detachment, and later on, he worked as a crime inspector in the police station, after which he was head for national security, and later on again, he was in charge of another municipality, and later, assistant commander of the brigade for moral guidance, religious issues, information, propaganda, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Simo Zaric, in what municipality --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Well, also for municipality number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that we go briefly into closed session just to deal with some characteristics of this municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to draw your attention to the period of the late 1991 and early of 1992. Were there four military detachments formed in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the different -- the responsibilities generally of these four military detachments.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Well, the responsibilities of these four military detachments were to preserve the territory, safeguard the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where did the men staffing these four detachments come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: The members of those four detachments were the local population from these three municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where did the equipment and arms used by these detachments come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: They came from the warehouse of the Yugoslav People's Army which was located in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to late February, early March of 1992. Did you have occasion to make a business trip on private business to Belgrade during that time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did somebody ask to accompany you on that trip?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: The person under number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And while on that trip, did you meet some other people in the company of number 13?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: After I had completed my meeting, I met for a short -- a brief period two other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: They were the gentlemen -- they were the gentleman under number 24 and the gentleman Milan Prodanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Milan Prodanic, what governmental organisation did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: He belonged to the state security of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the person you've described as number 24 from tab 3, what governmental organisation did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: He belonged to the Military Intelligence Service in the Federal Secretariat for National Defence in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you know that Mr. Prodanic worked for the State Security Service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: When I first met him personally, he just introduced himself by giving his name. However, upon my return, this other gentleman, the gentleman under number 13, told me where he worked and what his job was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the way back from Belgrade, back to your municipality, did the person you've identified as number 13, did he have a conversation with you about a decision that was taken with those other men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: He said that he would be sending some 20 men for training and asked me if I knew some young men who were willing to undergo such training, and if so, could I help him in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When he used the word "training," what was your understanding of who was conducting the training and what was the training for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Well, I understood later on that this was - how shall I put this? - military training, and it was conducted in an improvised camp, and later on I learned that that particular camp was organised by the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you know at that time where the camp was to be set up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: I didn't know at that time, but I learnt later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where did you learn that the camp was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: I don't know where it was supposed to have been located, but I learnt later on where it was located in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please tell us where that was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: It was in the surroundings of Ilok, Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after returning to your municipality, were men in fact selected and sent for training at this camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you identify the process that was used to identify the men sent for training at this camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Well, first of all, these people had to want to go on a voluntary basis. The second requirement was that they were under 30 years of age, and thirdly, that they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately when did these men leave your municipality and go to Ilok for this training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Well, they left sometime towards the end of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you had a second contact with members of the MUP of Serbia regarding the training of men from your municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the circumstances under which you had this second contact.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Well, sometime towards the end of March or in early April, the gentleman under number 13, as he heard that I was going to Belgrade, asked me to visit those young men that were doing their training and to try and make it to the training session, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how were you -- or who were you to see in order to be given access to this training facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Number 13 told me to get into contact with Mr. Milan Prodanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did you go to see Mr. Prodanic for the purpose of going to the training camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: I went to the building of the MUP of Serbia. Actually, the information desk, reception area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ask for him by name and where did he come to meet you at that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Yes. At the reception desk I introduced myself and asked to see the gentleman, and after some time had gone by, he came down to the ground floor. We went into a room that was opposite the reception desk, and I told him why I had come, what my business was. And later on, he sent me to visit those men that were doing their training.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he describe to you how you were to get to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: Well, at first I didn't know where they actually were, but he said a car of ours and some people are going there he said. So he introduced me to a man who was going there and he said, "They're going there, so you can follow their car, and you'll arrive at the place where the training was being conducted."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who of note was in that car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1244
utterances.text: In the car was Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Had you met Frenki Simatovic prior to this day?
